goal: Scrooge has no agency of his own — he is conducted as a witness; his operative goal is to understand what he is seeing, to locate himself in the scene and orient to its meaning

goal: Scrooge enters the scene as a passive witness — he has no explicit objective, but his implicit goal is to find some evidence that his death will matter to someone, or at least that the Phantom's revelations hold some limit of cruelty.
conflict: The scene itself opposes this goal: every element of what the Phantom shows him is evidence not of grief but of relief — the family's joy is not suppressed, it is barely apologized for. There is nothing here for Scrooge to hold onto.
crisis: Scrooge must either accept that his death has produced only happiness in people he has damaged, or ask the Phantom directly for something that contradicts everything he has just witnessed — he must choose between silence and plea.
decision: He speaks — he petitions the Phantom to show him tenderness connected with a death, naming the alternative (the dark chamber) as something he cannot bear to carry forever.

goal: To passively witness a memory — Scrooge enters as observer, wanting only to watch the past; he has no conscious objective beyond enduring what the Ghost shows him.

key_dialogue: "It's humbug still!"; "I won't believe it."
emotions: restless agitation; creeping inexplicable dread at the bell's movement; mounting alarm as the clanking rises through the building; a braced verbal defiance as the ghost passes through the door; involuntary shock as the flame leaps; a strange compelled attention as he examines the chain and the transparent body; determined resistance fighting directly against what his eyes report
motifs: the disused bell swinging softly then violently — sensation precedes belief, the body responds before the mind consents; the clanking chain heard before it is seen, rising floor by floor — dread that announces itself and cannot be outrun; the chain wound about Marley's middle like a tail, made of cash-boxes, keys, padlocks, ledgers, deeds, and purses — objects of commerce forged into bondage; the dying flame leaping at the ghost's entrance — the room itself recognizes what Scrooge refuses to; the transparent body through which coat-buttons are visible — the uncanny made specific and mundane; the folded kerchief bound about Marley's head and chin — a detail Scrooge had not observed before, noticed now with the helpless precision of a mind that is recording everything against its will
subtext: Scrooge says "I won't believe it" but his changing colour and compelled catalogue of the ghost's details show he already does; don't state this

goal: The narrator's goal is to certify Marley's death so completely that no reader can escape the supernatural premise; Scrooge's goal, enacted in memory, is to conduct business on the day of the funeral and to keep all human sympathy at maximum distance
conflict: The narrator must overcome the reader's natural impulse to rationalize a ghost story away; Scrooge's miserliness is opposed only by the ambient pressure of human warmth — beggars, children, passersby — which he defeats without effort
crisis: The narrator faces an implicit irreconcilable: to make a ghost story credible, he must insist on the reality of death while simultaneously preparing the reader to believe in the dead returning — he cannot have both unless he earns the supernatural through the relentless over-certification of the natural
decision: The narrator decides to acknowledge the absurdity of the "dead as a door-nail" simile openly, mock himself for it, defend it anyway on grounds of ancestral wisdom, and thereby convert his own unreliability into a bond of conspiratorial trust with the reader
key_actions: The narrator opens mid-declaration rather than mid-action, asserting Marley's death before the story has begun; narrator lists the four legal witnesses to the burial register; narrator names Scrooge as the fifth signer and immediately glosses his signature's commercial credibility; narrator interrupts himself to interrogate the "dead as a door-nail" simile, prefers "coffin-nail" on logic, defers to ancestral wisdom, then repeats the original simile emphatically; narrator explains that Scrooge knew Marley was dead because he was sole executor, administrator, assign, residuary legatee, friend, and mourner; narrator notes Scrooge conducted excellent business on the day of the funeral and found an undoubted bargain in it; narrator uses the mention of the funeral as a formal hinge to restate the death-certainty thesis; narrator invokes Hamlet's Father as the structural reason the death must be certified; narrator notes Scrooge never painted out Marley's name above the warehouse door and answered to both names indifferently; narrator delivers the comprehensive catalogue of Scrooge's miserliness in a single paragraph of accumulating adjectives; narrator maps the cold outward from Scrooge's interior onto his physical features; narrator argues that external weather had no power over Scrooge and that he was bitterer than any wind; narrator observes that no one spoke to Scrooge in the street, no beggars importuned him, no children asked him the time, even blind men's dogs pulled their owners into doorways at his approach; narrator notes Scrooge actively enjoyed this isolation — it was "nuts" to him
key_dialogue: "MARLEY was dead: to begin with. There is no doubt whatever about that."; "Mind! I don't mean to say that I know, of my own knowledge, what there is particularly dead about a door-nail."; "my unhallowed hands shall not disturb it, or the Country's done for."; "This must be distinctly understood, or nothing wonderful can come of the story I am going to relate."; "No wind that blew was bitterer than he, no falling snow was more intent upon its purpose, no pelting rain less open to entreaty."; "They often 'came down' handsomely, and Scrooge never did."; "No eye at all is better than an evil eye, dark master!"; "To edge his way along the crowded paths of life, warning all human sympathy to keep its distance, was what the knowing ones call 'nuts' to Scrooge."
emotions: conspiratorial warmth — the narrator pulls the reader close with a shared joke about similes; mock-scholarly self-importance — the narrator inflates the door-nail digression into a constitutional matter; dry amusement shading into something colder — Scrooge's conduct at the funeral is presented as a punchline that is also a verdict; gathering disgust — the catalogue of Scrooge's physical coldness accumulates past comedy into revulsion; dark comic relief — the weather comparisons restore ironic distance just as the portrait becomes unbearable; a final beat of bleak recognition — Scrooge's satisfaction in his own isolation is the scene's lowest note, the value fully negative

goal: Scrooge observes passively, trying to understand who has died and why the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come has brought him here
conflict: The scene offers no person to question, no action to take — only overheard conversation Scrooge cannot redirect or escape
crisis: Scrooge must stand and listen as men who knew him dismiss his death with yawns, jokes about lunch, and relief over black gloves — with no avenue for self-defense or intervention
decision: Scrooge looks toward the Spirit for an explanation rather than confronting what he has heard
key_actions: The city springs up around Scrooge and the Spirit without transition; the Spirit stops beside a small group of businessmen on the Exchange; Scrooge advances to listen; the men establish that someone familiar to them has died the previous night; they speculate briefly about the money; they joke about attending the funeral only if lunch is provided; the most familiar among them claims the dead man was his "most particular friend" because they used to stop and speak; the group dissolves into the larger crowd; Scrooge recognizes the men and turns to the Spirit for explanation
key_dialogue: "No, I don't know much about it, either way. I only know he's dead."; "What has he done with his money?"; "I haven't heard. Left it to his company, perhaps. He hasn't left it to me. That's all I know."; "It's likely to be a very cheap funeral, for upon my life I don't know of anybody to go to it. Suppose we make up a party and volunteer?"; "I don't mind going if a lunch is provided. But I must be fed, if I make one."; "Well, I am the most disinterested among you, after all, for I never wear black gloves, and I never eat lunch. But I'll offer to go, if anybody else will. When I come to think of it, I'm not at all sure that I wasn't his most particular friend; for we used to stop and speak whenever we met. Bye, bye!"
emotions: detached curiosity as Scrooge advances to listen; growing unease as the conversation reveals total indifference to the dead man; dawning dread as the jokes accumulate; mute incomprehension as the men disperse and Scrooge turns to the Spirit
motifs: money-chinkling and watch-checking in the background crowd before the conversation begins; the yawn repeated twice by the fat man — indifference made physical; the snuff-box as an object of attention during discussion of a death; the great gold seals the merchants trifle with; the joke about black gloves — mourning dress as a cost to be avoided
subtext: The fat man claims the dead man was his "most particular friend" because they spoke when they met; don't state what his laughter reveals about that friendship

goal: Scrooge has no conscious goal entering this scene — he is carried here involuntarily by the Ghost; his implicit goal becomes staying as long as possible once the warmth takes hold
conflict: His own emotional armor — the habitual coldness and contempt for fellowship — resists what the scene is forcing him to feel; he cannot participate, only observe; and the Spirit removes him before he is ready to leave
crisis: He must either remain detached and confirm his self-conception as a man who needs no one, or surrender to the joy of this household and acknowledge what his refusal has cost him
decision: He surrenders — he laughs aloud, guesses at the games, begs the Spirit for more time, and would have toasted his nephew if he could
key_actions: Scrooge is transported mid-brooding thought from dark isolation into Fred's lit, warm room; Fred laughs uproariously at the memory of Scrooge calling Christmas a humbug; the party discusses Scrooge's wealth as useless to him and to others; Fred's niece plays a harp tune that was familiar to young Scrooge at the boarding school, softening him further; the party plays blind-man's buff, with Topper pursuing the plump sister with transparent pretense; Scrooge joins in the game of Yes and No, calling out guesses aloud though no one can hear him; the party deduces the animal in Yes and No is Scrooge himself; Fred proposes a toast to Uncle Scrooge; Scrooge attempts to pledge the toast in return; the Ghost removes him before the scene ends
key_dialogue: "He said that Christmas was a humbug, as I live!"; "His wealth is of no use to him. He don't do any good with it. He don't make himself comfortable with it."; "I am sorry for him; I couldn't be angry with him if I tried. Who suffers by his ill whims! Himself, always."; "I mean to give him the same chance every year, whether he likes it or not, for I pity him."; "It's your Uncle Scro-o-o-o-oge!"; "Here is a new game. One half hour, Spirit, only one!"; "A Merry Christmas and a Happy New Year to the old man, whatever he is! He wouldn't take it from me, but may he have it, nevertheless. Uncle Scrooge!"
emotions: startled displacement — brooding darkness replaced without warning by warmth and laughter; guarded detachment, Scrooge observing from behind his habitual armor; the armor begins to give as laughter proves contagious; the harp tune breaks something open — grief for the self he might have been surfaces; unguarded delight as he shouts guesses at the game, forgetting himself entirely; the shock and sting of hearing himself named as the disagreeable animal; involuntary tenderness as Fred toasts him with genuine warmth; wistful longing and protest as the scene is snatched away before he is ready
motifs: contagious laughter spreading through the room like a physical force, catching even those who resist; the firelit, lamplit room as a warm enclosure opposed to the dark abyss Scrooge was traversing when the scene begins; the harp's simple air linking present warmth to the lost child at the boarding school; the blindfold in blind-man's buff — false not-seeing as cover for desire; the toast of mulled wine raised toward a man who cannot receive it
subtext: Fred praises Scrooge with pity and invites him yearly; don't state that Fred sees through Scrooge's hardness to the man who could still be saved

goal: Scrooge wants to end Fred's visit and return to solitary work without engaging with Christmas or accepting the dinner invitation.
conflict: Fred refuses to be dismissed, counters every argument with good humor, and keeps pressing — first for agreement, then for the dinner invitation, then simply for friendship.
crisis: Fred strips away every rationalization — no quarrel, no debt, no ask — leaving Scrooge with no logical ground to refuse friendship; he can only refuse by naked will.
decision: Scrooge chooses pure withdrawal, repeating "Good afternoon" as a wall rather than an argument, refusing to engage even when engagement would cost him nothing.
key_actions: Fred enters glowing and warm from rapid walking in cold fog; Scrooge answers the greeting with "Bah!" and "Humbug"; Fred parries Scrooge's "you're poor" with "you're rich enough"; Scrooge delivers the boiling-pudding speech; Fred makes the Christmas-as-fellowship speech; Cratchit involuntarily applauds then extinguishes the fire; Scrooge threatens Cratchit's position; Fred issues the dinner invitation; Scrooge refuses with an obscene go-to-the-devil expression; Fred asks why, pressing through each answer; Scrooge repeats "Good afternoon" four times until Fred leaves; Fred stops at the outer door to exchange warm greetings with Cratchit; Scrooge mutters about Cratchit talking of merry Christmas on fifteen shillings a week.
key_dialogue: "Merry Christmas! What right have you to be merry? What reason have you to be merry? You're poor enough."; "Come, then. What right have you to be dismal? What reason have you to be morose? You're rich enough."; "every idiot who goes about with 'Merry Christmas' on his lips, should be boiled with his own pudding, and buried with a stake of holly through his heart."; "Christmas among the rest. But I am sure I have always thought of Christmas time… as a good time; a kind, forgiving, charitable, pleasant time; the only time I know of, in the long calendar of the year, when men and women seem by one consent to open their shut-up hearts freely"; "I want nothing from you; I ask nothing of you; why cannot we be friends?"; "Good afternoon." (×4); "I'll retire to Bedlam."
emotions: Defensive irritation at the interruption; contemptuous certainty when delivering the economic argument against Christmas; momentary speechlessness when Fred parries with "you're rich enough"; indignant heat during the boiling-pudding speech; stern authority when threatening Cratchit; dismissive sarcasm when calling Fred a powerful speaker; reflexive disgust at the mention of love as a reason for anything; cold withdrawal behind the repeated "Good afternoon"; isolated self-satisfaction hardening into muttered contempt as he watches Cratchit warmly farewell Fred.
motifs: Fred's body as living rebuke to cold — ruddy face, sparkling eyes, steaming breath, the glow of rapid walking in frost; the fog and frost outside pressing against the warmth Fred carries in; the fire in the Tank, briefly animated by Cratchit's applause and then extinguished by his own hand; Scrooge's repeated "Good afternoon" as a door closed four times over; Fred's departure pausing at the outer door — the threshold between Scrooge's world and the warmer world outside.
subtext: Scrooge constructs elaborate economic arguments against joy but falls silent when Fred mirrors them back; don't state that the arguments are self-defense.

goal: Scrooge's goal is to meet the second spirit on his own terms — to be awake, positioned, and psychologically prepared so that he challenges the spirit at the moment of its appearance rather than being ambushed.
conflict: The spirit does not appear on schedule; instead an unexplained blaze of ruddy light fills the room, offering nothing to confront, interpret, or defend against — opposition that Scrooge's strategy of readiness cannot address.
crisis: A best-bad-choice between remaining in bed paralyzed by inexplicable light he cannot decipher or act against, and rising to investigate a source that might be more dangerous than any ghost he had steeled himself to face.
decision: Scrooge gets up, shuffles to the door, and puts his hand on the lock — choosing to move toward the unknown rather than endure passive dread.
key_actions: Wakes mid-snore and registers the bell striking one without being told; pulls back all the bed-curtains himself before lying down again; lies scanning every quarter of the room to preempt surprise; waits through five minutes, ten minutes, a quarter hour with no apparition; trembles violently when nothing arrives; endures the unexplained ruddy light streaming across his bed; fears he may be a case of spontaneous combustion; reasons, finally, that the light originates in the adjoining room; rises softly and shuffles in his slippers to the door; puts his hand on the lock; obeys a strange voice that calls his name and bids him enter.
key_dialogue: "a strange voice called him by his name, and bade him enter"
emotions: Wary self-possession and deliberate readiness as he pulls back the curtains himself; vigilant alertness as he scans the room; a violent fit of trembling when nothing appears; mounting alarm as the inexplicable light persists without shape or explanation; apprehension shading toward the grotesque as he entertains the spontaneous combustion thought; slow, reluctant reasoning toward action; cautious physical resolve as he rises and moves to the door.
motifs: The bell striking one — heard internally, without need of announcement; the bed-curtains pulled back by Scrooge's own hands rather than a spirit's; the blaze of ruddy light with no body or source, streaming across the bed; the slippers shuffling softly across the floor toward the door; the hand on the lock.
subtext: Scrooge performs readiness by opening the curtains himself but means to reclaim the dignity the first spirit stripped from him; don't state the reclamation.

goal: Scrooge wants to buy the prize turkey and have it delivered anonymously to Bob Cratchit's house in Camden Town.
conflict: No meaningful opposition — the conflict is entirely internal friction: shaking hands, breathless excitement, a body that can barely keep pace with the joy flooding through it.
crisis: None in the dramatic sense — the scene withholds crisis deliberately. Scrooge has already made every hard choice; this scene is the consequence of those choices flowing freely.
decision: Scrooge decides to send the turkey anonymously rather than claiming the gift — the generosity is the point, not the credit.
key_actions: Scrooge calls down to a boy passing in the street; asks whether the prize turkey is still hanging at the poulterer's; instructs the boy to go buy it and return with the delivery man; promises the boy a shilling, then half-a-crown if he returns in under five minutes; boy departs at a run; Scrooge whispers to himself that he will send it to Bob Cratchit's anonymously; writes the address with a trembling hand; goes downstairs to wait at the street door; notices and pats the door knocker; receives the turkey and declares a cab is necessary to carry it to Camden Town; pays for the turkey, the cab, and tips the boy, chuckling at each transaction; sits back in his chair and laughs until he cries; shaves badly with shaking hands, dresses in his best, and goes out into the streets; receives Christmas greetings from strangers and returns them.
key_dialogue: "An intelligent boy! A remarkable boy! Do you know whether they've sold the prize Turkey that was hanging up there?--Not the little prize Turkey: the big one?"; "What a delightful boy! It's a pleasure to talk to him. Yes, my buck!"; "Go and buy it, and tell 'em to bring it here, that I may give them the direction where to take it. Come back with the man, and I'll give you a shilling. Come back with him in less than five minutes and I'll give you half-a-crown!"; "I'll send it to Bob Cratchit's! He sha'n't know who sends it. It's twice the size of Tiny Tim. Joe Miller never made such a joke as sending it to Bob's will be!"; "I shall love it, as long as I live! I scarcely ever looked at it before. What an honest expression it has in its face! It's a wonderful knocker!--Here's the Turkey! Hallo! Whoop! How are you! Merry Christmas!"; "Why, it's impossible to carry that to Camden Town. You must have a cab."
emotions: giddy disbelief at his own happiness; warm delight in the boy's quickness; mounting private hilarity at the joke of the secret gift; physical overflow of joy the body cannot contain; tender wonder at the door knocker; explosive, breathless, weeping laughter; soft satisfied exhaustion; unsteady gladness during shaving; expansive public warmth toward strangers in the street.
motifs: the prize turkey measured against a child's body ("as big as me"), establishing scale as a form of generosity; the shaking, unsteady hand that cannot write the address steadily yet writes it anyway; the door knocker, patted and praised as an old friend newly seen; the chuckle repeated four times across a single sentence as an accumulating rhythm; dressing "all in his best" as outward expression of inward renewal; walking with hands behind him as an echo of the Ghost of Christmas Present's posture.
subtext: Scrooge insists the turkey go unsigned; don't say he fears being seen as changed — let the anonymity speak.

goal: Maintain composure and rational control by dismissing Marley's ghost as a sensory hallucination, thereby avoiding confrontation with the supernatural and its implications
conflict: The ghost's physical reality keeps asserting itself against Scrooge's defenses — its infernal atmosphere, its stony gaze, its ability to perceive what Scrooge holds up, and finally its terrifying physical demonstration when it drops its jaw
crisis: The ghost has proven its reality beyond rational argument and now offers Scrooge a "chance and hope" — but that chance requires submitting to three visitations Scrooge would rather refuse
decision: Scrooge accepts the visitations — not willingly, but because Marley makes clear there is no alternative to his own fate
key_actions: Scrooge greets the ghost with caustic cold deflection; asks whether the ghost can sit, for practical reasons; mounts a sustained rational-skepticism defense using the beef-and-gravy argument; produces a toothpick as a diversionary prop to break the ghost's stare; clings to his chair when the ghost shrieks and shakes its chain; falls to his knees when the ghost removes its head bandage and its jaw drops; questions Marley about the nature of his chain; attempts to reframe Marley's torment in business-like terms ("You must have been very slow about it, Jacob"); pleads for comfort Marley cannot give; receives the warning of three spirits; tries to negotiate taking all three at once; receives the schedule of visitations and Marley's departure
key_dialogue: "There's more of gravy than of grave about you, whatever you are!"; "You see this toothpick?"; "Mercy! Dreadful apparition, why do you trouble me?"; "I wear the chain I forged in life. I made it link by link, and yard by yard; I girded it on of my own free will, and of my own free will I wore it. Is its pattern strange to you?"; "Mankind was my business. The common welfare was my business; charity, mercy, forbearance, and benevolence, were, all, my business."; "I--I think I'd rather not"; "Couldn't I take 'em all at once, and have it over, Jacob?"
emotions: cold caustic confidence; willed flippancy masking rising terror; frantic verbal maneuvering to avoid meeting the ghost's gaze; physical dread breaking through the performance; collapse into kneeling terror; trembling humility while trying to reassert business-logic framing; dismayed quaking as Marley's grief escalates; faltering reluctant acquiescence
motifs: the chain — described as forged link by link, yard by yard, worn of free will, now ponderous and audible in the night; the dropped jaw and loosened head bandage — physical horror that defeats rational defense; the ghost's independent atmosphere — hair and tassels moving in unfelt heat; the toothpick — Scrooge's last prop of ordinary reality, turned absurd by the ghost's calm omniscience; Scrooge glancing at the floor expecting to see his own chain and seeing nothing
subtext: Scrooge reaches for jokes and props to look at rather than the ghost's eyes; don't state the terror the humor is hiding

goal: Escape the terrifying chamber and have the Ghost release him from the lesson
conflict: The Ghost refuses to move; its finger remains pointed unmovably at the shrouded head, and Scrooge lacks the power to lift the veil himself or compel the Spirit to relent
crisis: Best bad choice — Scrooge can either uncover the face and confirm what he fears (that the corpse is his own future self) or refuse and remain in unbearable, indefinite dread
decision: He refuses to lift the veil, pleads inability rather than unwillingness, and pivots to begging the Ghost to show him any person who feels grief at this death
key_actions: Scrooge recoils from the bed with the covered body; glances around the dark room in a searching, involuntary way; turns toward the Phantom and sees its finger pointing at the shrouded head; considers and physically longes to lift the sheet but finds himself unable to move his hand to do it; hears (internally, without voice) words meditating on the difference between a loved life and this unmourned one; registers the cat tearing at the door and rats gnawing beneath the hearthstone; asks the Ghost to let them leave; tells the Ghost he understands what it wants but confesses he lacks the power to act; begs the Ghost to show him anyone in the town who feels grief at this man's death
key_dialogue: "Spirit! this is a fearful place. In leaving it, I shall not leave its lesson, trust me. Let us go!"; "I understand you, and I would do it, if I could. But I have not the power, Spirit. I have not the power."; "If there is any person in the town, who feels emotion caused by this man's death, show that person to me, Spirit, I beseech you!"
emotions: Recoiling physical terror at the proximity of the corpse; compulsive, anxious searching of the dark room; paralyzed longing — wanting to lift the veil yet unable to move; a brief inward surge of pathos and moral reckoning provoked by the contrast between a loved death and this one; cold horror at the scavenging animals; desperate urgency to flee; helpless frustration at his own impotence before the Ghost's demand; agonized pleading for any evidence of human connection
motifs: The ragged, carelessly adjusted sheet that neither fully conceals nor reveals; the Ghost's unmoved, pointing finger that does not waver regardless of Scrooge's words; the pale light falling straight on the bed while the room remains too dark to read; the cat at the door and the rats beneath the hearthstone as the only living presences attending the corpse
subtext: Scrooge claims he lacks the power to lift the veil; he means he cannot bear to confirm what he suspects

goal: Close the counting-house and get away without conceding anything to Cratchit — particularly not Christmas Day with good grace
conflict: The social expectation of Christmas generosity directly opposes Scrooge's economic worldview; granting the day feels, to him, like theft from his own pocket
crisis: Scrooge cannot legally or socially refuse Christmas Day, so his only choice is whether to grant it with cruelty or with any scrap of decency
decision: He grants it while refusing decency — reframing the holiday as pocket-picking, demanding early arrival the next morning, and leaving with a growl rather than a word
key_actions: Scrooge dismounts his stool with ill-will; Cratchit instantly snuffs his candle and puts on his hat; Scrooge challenges Cratchit about wanting the day; Scrooge buttons his coat to the chin while accusing Cratchit of theft; Scrooge grants the full day with the condition of earlier arrival; Scrooge walks out with a growl; Cratchit closes the office in a twinkling; Cratchit goes down a slide on Cornhill with a lane of boys twenty times; Cratchit runs home to Camden Town to play blindman's-buff
key_dialogue: "You'll want all day to-morrow, I suppose?"; "If quite convenient, sir."; "It's not convenient, and it's not fair. If I was to stop half-a-crown for it, you'd think yourself ill-used, I'll be bound?"; "And yet, you don't think me ill-used, when I pay a day's wages for no work."; "A poor excuse for picking a man's pocket every twenty-fifth of December!"; "But I suppose you must have the whole day. Be here all the earlier next morning."
emotions: Scrooge's grinding, calculating resentment as he dismounts; Cratchit's careful, faint-smiled restraint under interrogation; Scrooge's self-righteous indignation at having to yield; Scrooge's impotent growl as he exits; Cratchit's instantaneous, unguarded, physical delight the moment Scrooge is gone
motifs: The snuffed candle — light extinguished by Scrooge's presence, instantly; Scrooge's great-coat buttoned to the chin — armoring against any warmth; Cratchit's white comforter dangling for want of a great-coat — cheerful poverty against Scrooge's muffled miserliness; the slide on Cornhill — spontaneous, repeated, communal joy as answer to the counting-house
subtext: Scrooge frames Christmas as robbery but means he cannot bear that something exists that money cannot cancel; don't state the meaning

goal: Scrooge aims to conduct his counting-house business undisturbed on Christmas Eve while keeping all expenditures — coal, warmth, light — at minimum.
conflict: The cold itself, which presses on everyone including Scrooge's clerk, creates implicit pressure toward ordinary human generosity; the clerk's visible suffering stands as a mute, continuous rebuke to Scrooge's control of the coal-box.
crisis: The clerk needs heat to function; Scrooge can provide it at trivial cost; granting it would be the natural, human act — but granting it would mean yielding the coal-box, which is the symbol and instrument of his dominion.
decision: Scrooge keeps the coal-box in his own room and makes clear that any approach to it will end in dismissal, so the clerk does not approach it.
key_actions: Scrooge sits working in the counting-house while cold and fog press in from outside; keeps the counting-house door open to watch the clerk; maintains a small fire for himself; holds the coal-box in his own room, out of the clerk's reach; the clerk attempts to warm himself at a candle and fails
key_dialogue: [No direct spoken dialogue appears in this scene; the threat is conveyed structurally rather than through speech — Scrooge's rule is so established that the mere approach with a shovel is enough to predict dismissal]
emotions: flat occupational absorption (Scrooge at work, untroubled); ambient proprietorial vigilance (the open door, the watching); the clerk's silent, resigned improvisation (the white comforter, the candle); the narrator's dry, ironic distance throughout
motifs: coal and the coal-box as instrument of dominion; fog pouring through every chink and keyhole, obscuring the houses opposite into mere phantoms; candles flaring in neighboring windows like ruddy smears on palpable brown air; the clerk's "dismal little cell" described as a sort of tank; the clerk's single coal of a fire against Scrooge's merely small one; the white comforter; the candle the clerk tries and fails to warm himself at
subtext: Scrooge keeps the door open to watch the clerk, but the watching enacts ownership, not supervision; don't state the ownership

goal: Scrooge needs to confirm that Christmas Day has not yet passed — that he still has time to act on his transformation.
conflict: His own disorientation; he has no way of knowing from inside his chambers whether the night of supernatural visitation consumed hours or days, and the urgency of that uncertainty is entirely internal.
crisis: Irreconcilable goods do not apply here — the crisis is simpler and more desperate: he must know the date before he can act at all, and he cannot know it alone.
decision: Scrooge calls down to a stranger in the street rather than wait, dress properly, or compose himself — he acts on raw need before dignity.
key_actions: Scrooge calls down from his window to a boy on the street below; the boy confirms it is Christmas Day; Scrooge repeats the date aloud to himself; Scrooge reasons aloud that the Spirits accomplished everything in a single night; Scrooge calls back down to the boy
key_dialogue: "What's to-day!"; "To-day! Why, CHRISTMAS DAY."; "It's Christmas Day! I haven't missed it. The Spirits have done it all in one night. They can do anything they like. Of course they can. Of course they can. Hallo, my fine fellow!"; "Hallo!"
emotions: frantic urgency as Scrooge calls down; suspended breathlessness waiting for the answer; flooding relief at the boy's confirmation; near-hysterical joy as Scrooge repeats the date and reasons through its meaning; warmth spilling outward toward the boy
motifs: the street below as the world Scrooge is about to re-enter; the boy in Sunday clothes as an ordinary life untouched by the night's ordeal; the window as the threshold between the transformed interior self and the unchanged external world

goal: To determine what this spirit is and what it wants from him, so he can orient himself and decide how to respond
conflict: The phantom offers no information — no speech, no face, no name confirmed, no acknowledged communication — only a pointing hand and absolute silence; Scrooge cannot negotiate, question, or appeal to anything recognizable
crisis: Scrooge fears this spirit more than any he has seen, yet he must choose whether to follow it into unknown future darkness — a best bad choice between remaining paralyzed by dread or surrendering to a force that will not speak to him, cannot be charmed, and may show him something he cannot survive seeing
decision: He speaks his transformation aloud, unprompted and unrewarded, then commands himself forward: "Lead on!"
key_actions: The phantom approaches slowly and silently, scattering gloom as it moves; Scrooge drops to his knee before it; Scrooge attempts to confirm the spirit's identity and purpose through questions; the phantom responds only by pointing, and once by a barely perceptible contraction of its garment; Scrooge's legs tremble and nearly fail him; the phantom pauses to let him recover, which worsens his horror rather than relieving it; Scrooge delivers an unprompted declaration of fear, purpose, and intent to change; Scrooge commands the phantom to lead on, twice; the phantom moves away and Scrooge follows in the shadow of its dress
key_dialogue: "I am in the presence of the Ghost of Christmas Yet To Come?"; "You are about to show me shadows of the things that have not happened, but will happen in the time before us. Is that so, Spirit?"; "Ghost of the Future! I fear you more than any spectre I have seen. But as I know your purpose is to do me good, and as I hope to live to be another man from what I was, I am prepared to bear you company, and do it with a thankful heart. Will you not speak to me?"; "Lead on! Lead on! The night is waning fast, and it is precious time to me, I know. Lead on, Spirit!"
emotions: Solemnity shading into dread as the phantom approaches; awe that forces him physically to his knees; urgent need to establish terms and meaning through questioning; renewed dread when the phantom pauses and he becomes conscious of invisible eyes watching him; willed courage summoned against the dread; terrified but deliberate surrender expressed as a command to himself as much as to the spirit

key_actions: Scrooge and the Spirit are transported instantly from the chamber to the city streets on Christmas morning; Scrooge watches workers shovel snow with joviality; the Spirit stands in a baker's doorway and lifts covers from dinner-carriers' dishes, sprinkling incense from his torch; when two carriers jostle and argue, the Spirit drops water on them and their anger dissolves; bells call people to church and the streets fill; Scrooge questions the Spirit about the torch's flavor and its effect on poor dinners; Scrooge levels the accusation that the Spirit would close bakers and shops on the seventh day; the Spirit denies it three times with increasing force; Scrooge retreats to indirect blame — "in your name, or at least in that of your family"; the Spirit distinguishes itself from those who act in its name through passion, pride, and selfishness; Scrooge promises to remember the distinction; they move on invisible into the suburbs
key_dialogue: "Is there a peculiar flavour in what you sprinkle from your torch?" / "There is. My own."; "Would it apply to any kind of dinner on this day?" / "To any kindly given. To a poor one most."; "Why to a poor one most?" / "Because it needs it most."; "I wonder you, of all the beings in the many worlds about us, should desire to cramp these people's opportunities of innocent enjoyment."; "I!" cried the Spirit.; "You would deprive them of their means of dining every seventh day, often the only day on which they can be said to dine at all."; "I seek!" exclaimed the Spirit.; "Forgive me if I am wrong. It has been done in your name, or at least in that of your family."; "There are some upon this earth of yours who lay claim to know us, and who do their deeds of passion, pride, ill-will, hatred, envy, bigotry, and selfishness in our name, who are as strange to us and all our kith and kin, as if they had never lived. Remember that, and charge their doings on themselves, not us."
emotions: detached wonder at the sudden transport and the city's improbable cheerfulness in grim weather; cautious curiosity as Scrooge probes the torch with measured questions; moral defensiveness as Scrooge pivots from wonder to accusation; chastened retreat as the Spirit's triple denial lands; halting accountability as Scrooge concedes the distinction and promises to remember it
motifs: the torch sprinkling incense on poor dinners — a priestly act of consecration directed downward toward the least; water from the torch dissolving anger between jostling carriers — charity as literal peacemaker; the thawed blotch of wet above each baker's oven steaming from the pavement — invisible warmth rising from shared labor; pot-bellied baskets of chestnuts and brown-faced onions given comic human life — abundance made friendly and democratic; the Spirit's gigantic body accommodating itself to any low roof with ease — immensity made humble

goal: Scrooge has no active goal entering this scene — he is transported involuntarily and tries to maintain emotional composure as he is dragged through a past he has suppressed
conflict: The landscape itself opposes his composure — the sensory flood of the countryside, the familiar gates and posts and trees, undoes his defenses faster than he can rebuild them
crisis: Scrooge cannot stop the involuntary grief rising in him, and he must choose between acknowledging it and hiding behind a transparent lie — his only defense is a word
decision: He lies — claims the moisture on his cheek is a pimple — then immediately surrenders that defense and asks to be led onward, choosing forward motion over continued pretense
key_actions: passes through the wall with the Ghost into open winter countryside; clasps hands together and cries out that he was bred here; the Ghost observes his trembling lip and wet cheek; Scrooge mutters that it is a pimple; asks the Ghost to lead him where it would; declares he could walk the road blindfold; walks along recognising every gate and post and tree; watches boys riding and calling to each other across snowy fields; the Ghost states the school is not quite deserted and a solitary child is left there still; Scrooge says he knew it and sobbed
key_dialogue: "I was bred in this place. I was a boy here!"; "Your lip is trembling. And what is that upon your cheek?"; [Scrooge mutters] "that it was a pimple"; "Remember it! I could walk it blindfold."; "Strange to have forgotten it for so many years!"; "These are but shadows of the things that have been. They have no consciousness of us."; "The school is not quite deserted. A solitary child, neglected by his friends, is left there still."
emotions: startled, disoriented wonder at the vanished city; sudden raw recognition — joy mixed with the pain of something suppressed for decades; a flooding sensory return that bypasses will; flustered defensiveness when the Ghost names his tears; a brief, false steadying; then unguarded fervour at the road he still knows by heart; confused involuntary gladness at the shouting boys; a baffled, self-interrogating anger at his own gladness; then collapse — grief admitted, the lie abandoned
motifs: the cold clear winter light replacing the city's darkness and mist; the thousand odours floating in the air, each connected to forgotten thoughts and hopes and joys and cares; the lip's trembling and the unnamed moisture on the cheek; every familiar gate and post and tree named as Scrooge passes them; the laughing, shouting boys filling the broad fields with merry music until the crisp air laughed; the solitary child left behind when all the others have gone home
subtext: Scrooge says it is a pimple but his whole body is weeping; don't state which

goal: Scrooge has no goal — he is a passive witness carried by the Ghost, unable to resist or redirect the journey
conflict: The scenes resist Scrooge's habitual frameworks; he cannot dismiss what he sees as comfortable sentiment or bourgeois ease — these people have nothing and still celebrate
crisis: Scrooge cannot reconcile his conviction that Christmas is hollow social performance with the evidence that men on a bleak moor, in a lighthouse, on an open sea choose it anyway, without audience or reward
decision: Scrooge does not decide — he can only look; his sole volitional act is holding the Ghost's robe as commanded
key_actions: the Ghost transports Scrooge without warning to a desolate moor; Scrooge asks where they are; they pass through the wall of a mud-and-stone hut; Scrooge witnesses a multi-generational family singing around a fire; the old man's voice rises when the family joins the chorus and sinks when they stop; the Ghost moves on before Scrooge can linger; Scrooge looks back and sees the last of the land disappear behind rocks; they land on a lighthouse built on a sunken reef; two scarred lighthouse keepers join hands and toast each other Merry Christmas; the elder keeper strikes up a song; the Ghost speeds on above the heaving sea to a ship far from shore; Scrooge stands beside the helmsman, lookout, and officers; every man on the ship hums a Christmas tune or speaks quietly of a past Christmas or thinks of someone far away
key_dialogue: "What place is this?"; "A place where Miners live, who labour in the bowels of the earth. But they know me. See!"; the old miner's Christmas song (unquoted, described as very old); the lighthouse keepers wishing each other "Merry Christmas" in their can of grog
emotions: dislocation and passive dread at the sudden transport to a barren moor; bewildered curiosity at the light in the hut window; arrested attention at the singing family; involuntary stirring at the old man's voice rising with the chorus; horror as the land vanishes and the sea opens; vertiginous awe at the lighthouse on its reef; something softening — not yet named — at the scarred keeper's song; quiet, inarticulate wonder watching the ship's crew murmur of home and remember distant people
motifs: firelight burning inside darkness (hut window against the moor; lighthouse ray against the awful sea; ship lanterns); song as the one warmth that costs nothing (the miner's old song; the keeper's gale-like hymn; the sailors' hummed tunes); the setting sun's "sullen eye" glaring at desolation before being swallowed by night; storm-birds rising and falling like the waves they skim; scarred and weathered surfaces (the moor's rude stones; the keeper's figure-head face); joining hands over a rough table; voices rising and falling in chorus

goal: Scrooge enters as a passive observer — carried by the Phantom — with no conscious objective; he is compelled to witness rather than to act
conflict: The scene will not let him remain a detached observer; the thieves' casual logic dismantles his ability to watch without recognizing himself
crisis: Scrooge must either continue watching and absorb what the thieves' logic means for his own life, or look away — but the Phantom gives him no escape
decision: He stays, listens, and finally speaks aloud his recognition: "The case of this unhappy man might be my own"
key_actions: Scrooge and the Phantom travel into a foul, low-reputation district Scrooge recognizes but has never entered; they arrive at Old Joe's rag-and-bone shop, a den of bought refuse; three figures — a charwoman, a laundress, and an undertaker's man — arrive independently and recognize one another with laughter; the man in faded black produces small items stripped from the corpse and receives a chalked total from Joe; Mrs. Dilber produces sheets, towels, silver teaspoons, boots; the charwoman produces bed-curtains taken rings-and-all while the body lay there; she produces the dead man's blankets; she produces his shirt, stripped from the corpse after someone had already dressed it for burial; Old Joe counts out their gains onto the floor; Scrooge listens in horror throughout; he shudders and speaks aloud to the Phantom
key_dialogue: "Let the charwoman alone to be the first! Let the laundress alone to be the second; and let the undertaker's man alone to be the third. Look here, old Joe, here's a chance!"; "Every person has a right to take care of themselves. He always did."; "If he wanted to keep 'em after he was dead, a wicked old screw, why wasn't he natural in his lifetime? If he had been, he'd have had somebody to look after him when he was struck with Death, instead of lying gasping out his last there, alone by himself."; "You don't mean to say you took 'em down, rings and all, with him lying there?" / "Yes I do. Why not?"; "He frightened every one away from him when he was alive, to profit us when he was dead! Ha, ha, ha!"; "Spirit! I see, I see. The case of this unhappy man might be my own. My life tends that way, now. Merciful Heaven, what is this!"
emotions: detached observation as Scrooge surveys the foul district from a remove; uneasy curiosity as the three thieves converge and laugh; rising unease as goods are spread and appraised with matter-of-fact cheerfulness; mounting horror as the bed-curtains are named and the circumstance of their taking sinks in; disgust and detestation as the shirt is produced and the charwoman describes stripping it from the corpse; shuddering self-recognition as the charwoman's explanation of the dead man's isolation lands as a description of Scrooge's own life
motifs: the rag-and-bone shop as a place where everything stripped of use or dignity is weighed and priced — keys, nails, bones, rags, and now a dead man's effects; the charcoal stove and smoky lamp as the only warmth in a scene otherwise cold with mercenary transaction; the chalked sums on the wall — lives reduced to arithmetic; the bed-curtains taken rings-and-all, their domestic intimacy made grotesque by the circumstance of taking; the shirt removed from a corpse already dressed for burial — the final dignity undone for a few pence; the flannel bag of coins emptied onto the ground as the scene's final image of what a life becomes
subtext: The charwoman justifies theft by saying the dead man drove everyone away; don't name that this is Scrooge's mirror

goal: Scrooge tries to identify whose future death the Ghost is showing him — reasoning his way toward a moral takeaway he can use for self-improvement
conflict: The Ghost gives him nothing — no speech, no explanation, only a pointed hand; the exchange between the two businessmen is so brief and content-free that it resists interpretation; Scrooge's own name never surfaces
crisis: Scrooge can read the scene as evidence that he is already changing (the hopeful interpretation) or as a mirror of his own life (the devastating one) — the text offers him both and he chooses the comfortable one
decision: he resolves to keep watching for his own image, trusting that his future self will clarify everything — he defers understanding rather than confronting what the scene is already telling him
key_actions: the Ghost leads Scrooge into a street and points at two men meeting; the two men exchange the shortest possible pleasantries and part; Scrooge notices the exchange seems trivial and reasons his way into patience; he looks for his own image in his accustomed corner and finds a stranger there; he registers his absence without alarm, attributing it to his new resolutions; he rouses himself from his reasoning and feels the Phantom's hand pointing at him; he shivers
key_dialogue: "How are you?" / "How are you?"; "Well! Old Scratch has got his own at last, hey?"; "So I am told. Cold, isn't it?"; "Seasonable for Christmas time. You're not a skater, I suppose?"; "No. No. Something else to think of. Good morning!"
emotions: detached curiosity as he tries to read the scene for moral instruction; mild impatience at the apparent triviality; settled confidence as he constructs a reassuring explanation; a flicker of surprise at his absent image, quickly suppressed; self-congratulation that his resolutions explain the gap; cold dread as the Phantom's hand turns toward him
motifs: the pointed hand of the Phantom, directing attention without explanation; cold as both weather comment and atmospheric register (spoken, felt, closing the scene); Scrooge's accustomed corner occupied by a stranger; the clock marking his usual hour with no Scrooge present
subtext: Scrooge hunts for a lesson that applies to someone else; don't state that the lesson is already him
